Issued at 206 PM CST Thu Nov 26 2026

Early this afternoon, a large upper-level low is centered over 
the Tennessee Valley. This storm is the product of two separate 
upper waves having phased together since last night into one 
cohesive storm system. It has a widespread footprint with 
afternoon satellite imagery showing a big majority of the US 
east of the Mississippi caught beneath its stratus. This system 
is responsible for a swath of rain that's slowly been expanding 
northwestward across the area and has recently extended to 
northwest of the I-55 corridor. Rain will continue stirring over
this same general area through the night tonight. Some further 
expansion northwestward toward Rockford is anticipated later 
today, but coverage across our northwest CWA looks to be more 
broken and generally lighter than farther east and southeast.

The storm system will slowly work northward across the OH 
valley and into the eastern Great Lakes by Friday. Models agree 
that quick pressure falls north and northwest of the low track 
will result in a region of dynamic cooling across portions of 
the lower Great Lakes which may bring a rain/snow mix to parts 
of northwest Indiana at times during the night. However, it's 
likely to remain predominantly rain while low level f-gen 
forcing in the storm's TROWAL may support periods of steadier 
light to moderate rainfall. There is surprisingly good agreement
on the distribution of QPF around the area with a majority of 
deterministic camps resolving near or over an inch across much 
of northwest Indiana from this evening through the end of Friday
morning. The rain will lighten up as it pulls away to the east 
late tonight through Friday morning.

In addition to the rain, this storm is also bringing blustery 
conditions to our Thanksgiving. Sites across the area have been 
regularly reporting 25 to 30 mph gusts since early afternoon. So
while temperatures are sitting in the lower and middle 40s, 
that wind is making it feel 5 to 10 degrees colder. A period of 
35 to 40 mph gusts may still be in the cards for later this 
afternoon and early evening, particularly near I-57 and east. 
Breezy north winds will stick around through the night and into 
Friday before easing later Friday.

Behind the storm, a brief period of upper height rises and deep
dry air advection amid a shortwave ridge will bring clearing 
skies to the latter half of Friday allowing some sunshine to 
sneak in for the afternoon. High temperatures will be very 
similar to today's in the middle and upper 40s.

Cloud cover will build again Friday night with the passing of a
low amplitude trough axis. Forcing from this feature will be 
meager, but a narrow plume of sufficient moisture along the 
trough axis in an otherwise dry ambient environment may support 
a brief push of light precip overnight. Chances are highest up 
north across WI where more ample low-mid level moisture will 
track and slightly stronger forcing via PVA is anticipated. 
Ensemble probabilities from the GEFS, ENS, and GEPS for a trace 
of precip are as high as 40 to nearly 50% across our north, 
while probs for anything measurable drop to below 15%. There is 
uncertainty in the low level thermal setup and most camps 
suggest a low level warm nose would point toward mostly 
sprinkles or very light rain, but a few cooler solutions would 
still suggest that some flurries may mix in as well. 
Accordingly, maintained "silent" PoPs (less than 15%) in the 
forecast while highlighting an area of sprinkles and possible 
flurries north of I-80 overnight into very early Saturday 
morning. Otherwise, Saturday will see highs in the lower 50s and
a fair mix of clouds and sun.

Over the weekend, a deep upper trough will dig across the 
Plains and Midwest and drive a low level circulation across the 
Mid-Mississippi and Ohio valleys. Widespread rain is anticipated
across the northern flank of the low and will fall on the CWA 
Saturday night into Sunday afternoon. While surface temperatures
should be safely above freezing during the day on Sunday, much 
cooler low level air in the storm's northwest quadrant may 
support a period of rain/snow mix as the system pulls away 
during the late afternoon and evening.

Monday looks to be the coolest day of the next week in the wake
of the weekend system with highs forecast around 40 degrees. 
The upper jet pattern early next week will be characterized by 
quiet zonal and split flow regimes, while low level return flow 
from an eastern US high will encourage a warming trend that 
looks to get us back into the 50s by the middle of next week. 
The synoptic pattern will become more active again during the 
latter part of next week with a series of waves progged to 
traverse the central CONUS, although nothing in the extended 
forecast stands out at this time.
